body.heading: Gas squeezed into a liquid
paragraphs: The fizz in a fizzy drink is carbon dioxide — the same gas you breathe out — forced into the drink at the factory. Gases dissolve better in liquids under pressure, so the bottling plant pumps the drink full of carbon dioxide at several times normal air pressure and seals it in. Trapped there, most of the gas stays dissolved and invisible, with a cushion of it sitting in the space above the drink, holding the pressure.

Twist the cap and you hear the escape: pressure drops to match the room, and suddenly the liquid is holding far more gas than it can keep at this pressure. The excess has to leave — as bubbles. That hiss, and the rising streams that follow, are the drink returning to balance.

body.heading: Where bubbles are born
paragraphs: Bubbles do not form just anywhere. A new bubble needs a starting point — a microscopic scratch in the glass, a fibre, a grain, or the rough surface of an ice cube — and gas gathers at these nucleation sites until bubbles grow large enough to break free and rise, expanding as the pressure around them falls.

This is why shaking a bottle makes such a mess: it breaks the gas into countless tiny bubbles spread through the drink, each one a seed that swells explosively when the cap opens. Warmth speeds everything up, because warm liquid holds less dissolved gas than cold — a warm bottle always erupts more than a chilled one.

body.heading: Why drinks go flat
paragraphs: Once opened, the escape never quite stops. Every pour, every bubble and every hour sitting open lets more carbon dioxide slip away, until the drink holds only as much as ordinary air pressure allows — which tastes like nothing. Flat cola is simply cola that has reached equilibrium with the room.

The extremes of fizz show the pressures involved. A bottle of champagne, refermented in the bottle itself, sits at around five or six times atmospheric pressure — which is why its cork is wired down, and why it can leave the bottle at the speed of a car on a motorway.

description: The fizz in a soft drink is carbon dioxide forced into the liquid under pressure, escaping the moment you open the bottle.
